## Overview

The Pare, also called Wapare in Swahili, are a Bantu ethnic group whose ancestral home is the Pare Mountains of Same District and Mwanga District in Tanzania’s Kilimanjaro Region. Their historic location lies on a northern route of East-African long-distance trade connecting the hinterland with the coast of the Indian Ocean. Pareland was historically known to its inhabitants as Vuasu in the south and Vughonu in the north. The southern population is known as Vaasu and speaks Chasu, also called Athu, while the northern population is known as Vaghonu and speaks Kighonu. Pare history includes iron production, irrigation, rain-making, centralized and clan-based political systems, initiation institutions, rotating markets, and interaction with neighboring Chaga, Maasai, Shambaa, Zigua, Taita, and Mbugu populations.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

They state only that spiritual figurines used in rain-making, healing, initiation, and other cultural practices were wrapped in cloth and/or leather.

### Architecture

They do document specialized irrigation systems in North Pare, including hundreds of irrigation intakes and furrows constructed during the period of Shana rule. These systems were negatively affected when responsibility for irrigation management shifted from patrilineages to village-level committees after independence.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Iron production was a major Pare activity. The Pare were the main producers of iron for which there was considerable demand from the Chaga, Maasai, and other adjacent populations. The Shana clan maintained blacksmithing expertise; *Shana* means “blacksmith.” Iron products included weapons made for neighboring markets, and the blacksmiths of Mamba in Kilimanjaro developed a specialization in producing weapons on a large scale.

Archaeological evidence includes iron-smithing activities and objects collected by Hans Fuchs in the early twentieth century in North Pare. These are held in the ethnographic collections of the Náprstek Museum in Prague. The sources also mention pottery in South Pare associated with Bantu-speaking communities and dated by radiocarbon evidence to well before the year 1000 A.D.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They do mention spiritual figurines artistically sculptured from clay or wood and wrapped in cloth and/or leather.

## Music & performance

They do document ritual specialists and ceremonial performances connected with rain-making, healing, and initiation. In these practices, spiritual figurines made from clay or wood were used and wrapped in cloth and/or leather.

Rain-making was associated with rulers and political authority. The Pare were known as rainmakers, and one notable exponent was Mfumwa Muhammad Kibacha Singo, a local ruler of Same who died in January 1981. In South Pare, rulers connected with rain-making and *kuhoja* held ceremonial influence. *Kuhoja* is described as the paranormal ability to shield people, domestic animals, and crops from illnesses and other disasters.

The sources also describe political and ritual institutions rather than music itself. In Kizungo, the ruler Kikwa was anointed as both ruler and rainmaker before being sent there. In Usangi, Chasimba, also known as Madiva, was ordained in Mbaga as a rain-maker and ceremonial leader before leading an army to the region. No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription or museum catalogue record supplied for this atlas concerns Pare music.

## Dance & theatre

They describe initiation, healing, rain-making, and other ritual practices.

## Festivals & rituals

They do document several ritual and political institutions. The Pare practiced initiation systems, and initiation was an important means of social organization in both North and South Pare.

Under the Suya dynasty, earlier clan initiation ceremonies became a complex state institution. The Ugweno initiation system was centralized and closed to outsiders, while South Pare initiation rites were administered by individual clans and were accessible to people who fulfilled the ritual requirements. South Pare communities also maintained diplomatic consultation through messengers carrying *kimalisa*, described as the royal whisk.

In South Pare, ritual authority was connected with rain-making and *kuhoja*. The latter concerned protection for people, domestic animals, and crops against illnesses and other disasters. The sources also mention spiritual figurines used in rain-making, healing, initiation, and related cultural practices. They state that Pare communities historically engaged in continuous economic cooperation through rotating markets and maintained several systems of political and ritual authority.

## Foodways

They do state that Pare markets supported trade with neighboring populations and that the Pare received livestock in exchange for their articles in transactions with the Shambaa, Chaga, and Maasai.

The sources describe *mbiru* as tribute and other payments due to a rain-maker ruler. They also mention domestic animals and crops in connection with *kuhoja*. No museum catalogue record supplied for this atlas documents Pare foodways.

## Oral tradition & literature

The supplied sources describe historical traditions concerning the origins, migrations, rulers, and political transformations of Pare communities.

Gweno traditions state that society was already fairly stratified by the time it was sixteen generations old, or around the start of the sixteenth century. Other accounts refer to rulers and migrations through generational descriptions. Pare traditions also remembered people who lived in the region before the current Pare population and referred to those early inhabitants unclearly as “Galla.”

The sources emphasize uncertainty and competing interpretations in the history of Ugweno and the Shana dynasty. They state that the disruption of Shana rule contributed to miscommunication of history among modern communities and to misinterpretations by early European adventurers and historians. No contemporary literary revival or preservation project is identified.

## Language & religion

Pare is a Northeast Coast Bantu language spoken by the Pare people of Tanzania. It is also known as Kipare, Asu, Casu, Chasu, Athu, and Chathu. The language distinguishes high and low tone; the dental fricatives /θ ð/ occur only in Swahili loanwords, and /m/ can be syllabic.

Pareland historically included Vuasu in the south and Vughonu in the north. The people of Vuasu are Vaasu and speak Chasu or Athu. The people of Vughonu are Vaghonu and speak Kighonu, also called Gweno in Swahili. Northern Pare includes the Gweno-speaking area of Ugweno and the Chasu-speaking area of Usangi. Interaction with the Ma'a, or Mbugu, people contributed to a mixed language described as combining Chasu grammar with Cushitic vocabulary. They do document rain-making, healing, initiation, ritual specialists, spiritual figurines, shrines, and *kuhoja*. They also describe religious shrines created in Bwambo to unite the population as the territory expanded.
